chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Emerging Market Crises of the 1990s

lessons.title: India's 1991 Balance of Payments Crisis: Gold Pledged, Economy Opened

body.text: In 1991, India came within weeks of defaulting on its foreign debt for the first time in its history. The crisis forced the country to pledge its gold, and then to tear down the economic system that had put it there.

children.text: In July 1991, the Reserve Bank of India quietly shipped 46.91 tonnes of gold out of the country and pledged it with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan, in exchange for a loan of $405 million. Two months earlier, 20 tonnes of government gold had already been sent to Union Bank of Switzerland through the State Bank of India. For a country where gold carries deep emotional weight, pawning the nation's gold was a public humiliation. It was also necessary. India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about $1.1 billion, enough to pay for only two to three weeks of imports.
This is the most important financial crisis in modern Indian history. Every rule about forex reserves, external debt and the rupee that the RBI follows today was shaped by it.

children.text: Build-up: A Decade of Borrowing
To understand 1991, you need two terms. The
balance of payments
tracks every rupee and dollar crossing India's borders. Within it, the
current account deficit
measures how much more India spends abroad than it earns.

markDefs.definition: A record of all money flowing between a country and the rest of the world: trade, remittances, investment and loans. A balance of payments crisis is when a country cannot find enough foreign currency to pay what it owes abroad.

The gap when a country pays more to the world for imports of goods and services, interest and other transfers than it earns from exports and remittances. The gap must be funded by foreign capital or by running down reserves.

children.text: Through the 1980s, both sides of the problem grew. The Centre's gross fiscal deficit stayed above 8% of GDP from 1985-86 onwards. The current account deficit widened from 2.3% of GDP in 1989-90 to 3.1% in 1990-91. To fund the gap, India turned increasingly to commercial borrowing and to deposits from non-resident Indians, much of it short-term money that could leave quickly.

body.text: The last row is the one that mattered most. Total debt tells you how heavy the load is. Short-term debt against reserves tells you whether you can survive if lenders refuse to roll over for even a few months. In 1991, India could not.

body.title: Go deeper: why NRI deposits and short-term credit are "hot money"

children.text: Not all foreign money is equally loyal. The kind of inflow a country relies on decides how fast a crisis can hit.

cells: Long-term concessional loans from the World Bank and governments
Very slowly; repaid over decades
Stays put
Foreign direct investment in factories and businesses
Slowly; plants cannot be sold overnight
Mostly stays put
NRI deposits in Indian banks
As fast as depositors can withdraw
Can leave the moment confidence cracks
Short-term trade credit and commercial loans
At the next rollover, often within months
Lenders simply refuse to renew

children.text: By 1990, India had leaned too heavily on the bottom two rows. When confidence broke, that money did exactly what hot money does.
Trigger: War, Instability and Downgrades

On 2 August 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait. For India, the damage arrived through three channels at once. Oil import costs jumped. Remittances from the Gulf, estimated at over $2 billion a year, were disrupted. And India had to evacuate its own people: between 13 August and 20 October 1990, Air India flew out about 1,70,000 Indians, still the largest evacuation ever carried out by a civil airline.

At home, politics made things worse. The V.P. Singh government fell in November 1990, and the minority Chandra Shekhar government that followed could not pass a full budget in February 1991 after a credit rating downgrade by Moody's. Lenders read the signals clearly: a country with falling reserves, rising debt and no stable government.

body.title: How Many Weeks Were Left?
body.prompt: India's imports in 1990-91 were about $24 billion. In June 1991, forex reserves were about $1.1 billion. Assuming imports ran at an even weekly pace, how many weeks of imports could the reserves pay for? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Weekly imports = $24 billion ÷ 52 = about $0.46 billion. Import cover = $1.1 billion ÷ $0.46 billion = about 2.4 weeks. That is the "two to three weeks of imports" figure you will see quoted for June 1991. Economists usually consider three months of import cover the bare minimum for comfort.

children.text: Panic: Why India Had to Pledge Its Gold

Once reserves fell this low, the usual sources of dollars closed. NRI depositors withdrew money. Commercial lenders refused to roll over short-term credit. A formal default on foreign debt would have cut India off from world markets for years and made even essential imports like oil and fertiliser hard to buy.

Gold was the one asset India held that foreign lenders would accept immediately. Pledging it was not a sale. It was collateral for a loan, much like taking a gold loan from a bank against family jewellery, except the borrower was the country itself.

body.label: The Gold Came Home
body.value: The pledge loan was repaid by November 1991
body.context: The RBI repaid the $405 million loan against its pledged gold between September and November 1991, within months of taking it. The pledge had done its job: it bought India time without a default.

body.title: Why Gold, and Why a Pledge?
body.question: In July 1991, why did the RBI pledge gold as collateral for a loan instead of simply printing more rupees to pay India's foreign debts?
options: Printing rupees was illegal under the RBI Act
Foreign lenders wanted dollars, not rupees, and gold was an asset they would accept immediately as security
Gold prices were at a record high, so selling was the most profitable choice
The IMF required India to hold no gold reserves
body.explanation: India's debts were owed in foreign currency. The RBI can create rupees, but it cannot create dollars, exactly the trap you saw with Sri Lanka in Chapter 1 and Latin America in Chapter 2. Gold is accepted everywhere as collateral, so pledging it let India borrow dollars quickly without defaulting, and keep the option to redeem the gold later.

children.text: Policy Response: Devalue, Borrow, Reform

The Rao government moved fast on three fronts. First, it devalued the rupee by about 18% in two steps on 1 and 3 July 1991, making Indian exports cheaper and imports dearer to shrink the current account deficit. Second, it secured IMF support. Third, and most importantly, it attacked the causes, not just the symptoms.
In his budget speech on 24 July 1991, Manmohan Singh closed by quoting Victor Hugo: "no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come". That idea was opening up the Indian economy.

body.title: Show me: what devaluation does to the current account

children.text: Take a simple illustration. Before devaluation, suppose the rupee is ₹20 per dollar. After an 18% devaluation, a dollar costs about ₹23.60.

cells: An Indian exporter sells a $1,000 shipment
Earns ₹20,000
Earns ₹23,600
Exporting becomes more profitable, so exports rise
An Indian importer buys a $1,000 machine
Importing becomes more expensive, so imports fall

children.text: More exports and fewer imports shrink the current account deficit. The cost is that imported essentials, especially oil, become dearer, which pushes up inflation. That is why devaluation alone was never enough, and had to come with reforms.

body.title: Name the 1994 Milestone
body.textWithBlank: In August 1994, India made the rupee convertible on the current ___, allowing it to be freely exchanged for trade, travel and other current transactions.
body.explanation: Current account convertibility. From August 1994, India accepted Article VIII of the IMF's Articles of Agreement, so rupees could be freely converted for imports, exports, travel, remittances and similar payments. Capital account transactions, like large overseas investments, remain partly controlled even today.

children.text: The contrast is not just a bigger number. The deepest lesson of 1991, that short-term foreign money can vanish in weeks, now shapes how the RBI thinks about reserves, external commercial borrowing limits and the rupee.

body.title: You Are the Finance Minister, June 1991
body.scenario: It is late June 1991. You have just taken office. Reserves are about $1.1 billion, short-term foreign debt is several times larger than foreign currency assets, NRI depositors are withdrawing money, and a large debt repayment is due within weeks. Your options include: default on foreign debt; print rupees and impose strict import bans; pledge gold for an emergency loan; devalue the rupee; seek IMF support; announce structural reforms.
body.prompt: Which options would you choose, in what order, and why would you reject the others?
body.modelAnswer: The order that worked in 1991 was roughly: raise emergency dollars first, fix the price second, fix the causes third. Step one, pledge gold and seek IMF support, because they bring in dollars within weeks and avoid default. Step two, devalue the rupee, so exports become more competitive and imports shrink, reducing the drain on reserves. Step three, announce structural reforms, such as ending industrial licensing, cutting tariffs and opening to foreign investment, so that lenders and investors see a credible reason to return and growth can pay down debt over time. Reject default, because it would cut India off from world credit for years and make oil and fertiliser imports hard to finance, hurting the poorest most. Reject printing rupees and banning imports as the main plan, because foreign debts are owed in dollars that the RBI cannot print, and severe import bans would choke industry and farming. Some import compression is unavoidable in a crisis, but on its own it treats the symptom and deepens the slump. Emergency liquidity buys time, but only reform removes the reason the crisis happened.

cards.definition: When a country cannot find enough foreign currency to pay for imports and service its foreign debt.
Spending more abroad on imports, interest and transfers than earning from exports and remittances.
How many weeks or months of imports a country's forex reserves could pay for. In June 1991, India had two to three weeks.
Foreign debt due within a year compared with foreign currency assets. India's was 382.1% at end-March 1991.
A deliberate cut in a currency's official value. India devalued the rupee by about 18% on 1 and 3 July 1991.
Freedom to exchange the rupee for foreign currency for trade and current payments. India adopted it in August 1994.
